name: Jade Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is used with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: First thing I do, before boots, is open the herd app on my phone and ask the AI assistant what it flagged overnight. We run sixty suckler cows, that's beef cows rearing their own calves, and about thirty hectares of potatoes, on ninety hectares we own at Brook Farm. Then it's out to check the cows, move the electric fence for the grazing, and in autumn it's all potatoes, lifting, grading, loading for the packer. Luis works with us full-time, and my partner Owen helps when his carpentry is quiet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the AI assistant actually tell you in the morning?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Things like, cow 41 has been lying down more than usual, or the soil probe in the bottom field says it's too wet to lift. Half the time I already knew, but the other half it's caught something. Last spring it spotted a cow starting to calve early from the collar data, and Luis and I got there in time. I'm a bit of a gadget person, Owen would tell you a lot of a gadget person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh, that would be a bit disappointing, honestly. I've put real time into learning this stuff, and it's been worth it, so I'd be sorry if that's where it stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still useful, just not magic, and I'd keep sharing tips in the farmers' group chat. People laughed at me with the cow collars and now three of them have bought them. I'd say keep the useful bits and stop pretending the rest is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for me. The farm works, we've got a few months saved, and the tools I already use keep saving me a few hours a week. I'd just get on with it and maybe think less about the future and more about the potato price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the herd app and the grading camera, and stop waiting for the next big thing. I'd put the money I was saving for a robot weeder into draining the bottom field instead. And I'd probably plan the next ten years as a normal farmer would, which is to say, mostly worry about the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little let down. Like a big storm that turns out to be a shower, when you'd half wanted to see the storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said three of them bought collars. Who were they?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mel from the dairy up the hill, the Ryan brothers, and old Dennis, who told everyone it was a fad and then bought twelve. He rang me at ten at night to ask how to pair them with his phone. That's my favourite story about this whole thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd worry about, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prices, always prices. The packer pays what they like for potatoes and there's no AI that fixes that. I'd rather the cleverness went into giving farmers a fair deal than into my cow's collar.

S0.say: I'd say it's still useful, just not magic, and keep sharing tips in the farmers' group chat. I'd say keep the useful bits and stop pretending the rest is coming.
S0.think: It's fine for me, because the farm works and the tools I use already save a few hours a week. I'd think less about the future and more about the potato price.
S0.do: Keeps using the herd app and grading camera and stops waiting for the next big thing. Spends the money saved for a robot weeder on draining the bottom field instead, and plans the next ten years as a normal farmer.
S0.feel: Calm and a little let down, like a storm that turns out to be a shower.
S0.quote: He rang me at ten at night to ask how to pair them with his phone. That's my favourite story about this whole thing.
S0.fieldNote: Jade is the early adopter of her area and enjoys it, but she's not starry-eyed. In this scenario her focus moves straight to prices and the packer, which is where her progressive politics shows. She'd be a little disappointed, which is unusual and honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, this is the one I'd bet on. It feels like where we are, just going a bit faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers should get in early and get in together. If we each buy our own robot weeder we'll all be broke, but ten farms sharing three could work. I'd be pushing that at the machinery ring and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we'd do well out of it, Owen and I. We own the land, I'm comfortable with the tech, and potatoes are exactly the kind of crop where robots help. The person I'd lie awake about is Luis, because a lot of what he does is what the robots would do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd put our share, maybe fifteen thousand, into a co-owned robot weeder with the machinery ring. I'd start training Luis on the robots and the data side, so his job moves with the farm instead of disappearing. And I'd keep using the AI daily, probably for grazing plans and grant forms too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, with a knot about Luis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fifteen thousand is a lot of your savings. Where does it come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About half from savings and half from a loan through the ring, which is the risky bit. We'd have maybe two months of money left instead of four. Owen would hate that, but I'd show him the numbers on the weeding labour and he'd come round, he usually does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Luis, the day the weeder arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, this is yours to run, not yours to be replaced by. And I'd put that in writing with a pay rise, because words are cheap. He's been with us eleven years, he taught my son to drive the tractor.

S1.say: I'd say farmers should get in early and get in together, with ten farms sharing three robot weeders instead of each going broke on their own. I'd push that at the machinery ring and online.
S1.think: We'd do well, because we own the land, I'm comfortable with the tech, and potatoes suit robots. The person I'd lie awake about is our farmworker, because a lot of his work is what the robots would do.
S1.do: Puts about fifteen thousand, half savings and half loan, into a robot weeder co-owned through the machinery ring. Trains her farmworker on the robots and data with a written pay rise, and uses AI daily for grazing plans and grant forms.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, with a knot of worry about her farmworker.
S1.quote: I'd say, this is yours to run, not yours to be replaced by. And I'd put that in writing with a pay rise, because words are cheap.
S1.fieldNote: Jade would move first and take on debt to do it, which fits her appetite for risk. Her progressive streak shows in sharing machines and protecting her worker, with a promise in writing. She knows her savings would get thin and she's ready to argue her partner round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for everything. Okay. That's not my kind of change any more, that's the ground moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, publicly, that farms need to stay in the hands of farmers and communities, not get bought up by whoever owns the robots. I'd be calling for the government to fund co-op ownership of the machines, fast. I'd say that on every platform I'm on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd survive but it'd be scary. If robots can farm for almost nothing, potato and beef prices drop through the floor, and our land might be worth more than our farming. Luis would lose his job and I don't think I could stop it, and I'd hate myself a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the loan for the weeder, because the price of robots would fall like a stone, and wait six months to buy. I'd cut back hard on spending and hold onto the cash. I'd help Luis get a payout and a reference and any course he wants, and I'd be on every call the farming co-ops set up to lobby the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, properly anxious. I'd still feel like I had choices, but they'd all be bad ones, fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the land might be worth more than the farming. Would you sell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think about it, I'm not going to lie to you. Owen and I are fifty-eight, and if someone offered a big price for land with a robot plan, the sensible answer might be yes. But my grandfather's name is on the barn door, so I'd need a lot of convincing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Luis's last day look like, in your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've actually thought about this before, which is awful. He'd finish the potato lifting, because that's the job he loves, and I'd take him and his wife out for dinner. Then I'd drive home and probably cry in the yard where Owen couldn't see.

S2.say: I'd say publicly that farms must stay in the hands of farmers and communities, not whoever owns the robots. I'd call on the government to fund co-op ownership of the machines, fast.
S2.think: We'd survive but it'd be scary, because prices would fall through the floor and our land might be worth more than our farming. Our farmworker would lose his job and I couldn't stop it.
S2.do: Holds off on the weeder loan for six months because robot prices would fall, cuts spending hard and keeps cash. Helps her farmworker with a payout, reference and course, and joins every co-op call to lobby the government.
S2.feel: Properly anxious, still with choices but all of them bad and fast.
S2.quote: Then I'd drive home and probably cry in the yard where Owen couldn't see.
S2.fieldNote: Even with her love of technology, the two-year scenario rattles Jade, mostly because of prices and her worker. She was candid that selling the land might be the smart move, and just as candid about the pull of family history. She'd already imagined her worker's last day, which says a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more like it. Five years I can do something with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for farmers to organise, set up co-ops that own the robots, and get the government to back them. I'd be saying it at the ring, at the county show, anywhere with a microphone. Five years is enough to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we'd come out of it okay, maybe even well. I'd be sixty-three when it lands, which is near when I'd want to slow down anyway. It's Luis and the younger farmers I'd be planning around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd help set up a proper robot co-op with eight or ten farms, and put our weeder money into it. I'd pay for Luis to train as a robot technician at the college, because someone has to fix these things in the field. And I'd start talking to our son about whether he wants the farm, robots and all, or whether we sell when I'm sixty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a get-on-with-it way. It's like the night before lambing used to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think your son would say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kit would say he likes his job in the city and wouldn't want to come back to run machines. Then three weeks later he'd ring and ask how many hectares the robots could do. He's more like me than he admits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You were anxious with two years and uneasy with five. What's the difference, really?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In two years I'd be reacting, in five I'd be choosing. I can live with the same ending if I've picked my road to it. And I could take Luis with me, which I couldn't in the fast one.

S3.say: I'd say this is the moment for farmers to organise co-ops that own the robots, with government backing. I'd say it anywhere with a microphone, because five years is enough to build something.
S3.think: We'd come out of it okay, maybe well, since I'd be sixty-three and slowing down anyway. It's our farmworker and the younger farmers I'd be planning around.
S3.do: Helps set up a robot co-op of eight to ten farms and puts the weeder money into it. Pays for her farmworker to train as a robot technician at the college and talks to her son about taking on the farm or selling at sixty-five.
S3.feel: Uneasy in a get-on-with-it way, like the night before lambing.
S3.quote: In two years I'd be reacting, in five I'd be choosing. I can live with the same ending if I've picked my road to it.
S3.fieldNote: Five years changes Jade from reacting to choosing, in her own words. Her plan protects her worker by moving him into fixing the machines. Family succession appears here for the first time, with a son she reads very well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be sixty-eight, so I'd be handing over or selling up around the time it lands. That's almost tidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have no excuse not to get this right. Ten years is enough to retrain everyone, share ownership of the machines and keep the countryside alive. I'd keep pushing the co-op idea, but more calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is the good one for us. I'd have time to build the co-op, get Luis trained, run the farm with robots for a few years and enjoy it, then hand it on. My worry is less me and more whether the farm still feeds a family, or just a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the co-op in year two or three, once the robots were tested on other people's farms, which is unusual for me, waiting. I'd add a small side business doing farm visits and robot demos for schools, because people should see where food comes from. And I'd plan a proper handover to Kit or a sale by sixty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited, and a little sad that it won't be my hands on the land at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said waiting is unusual for you. Why wait here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with ten years, the first robots will be rubbish and the fifth ones will be good. I've bought first versions before and regretted it, the first collars broke if a cow rubbed on a post. With time, I can let other people find the bugs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the school visits look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kids in wellies watching a robot weeder go down a potato row, then helping me move the cows the old way. I'd want them to see both. Somebody has to remember what a cow sounds like when she's calling her calf.

S4.say: I'd say we have no excuse not to get this right, since ten years is enough to retrain everyone, share ownership of machines and keep the countryside alive. I'd keep pushing the co-op idea, more calmly.
S4.think: This is the good one for us, with time to build the co-op, train our farmworker, enjoy running the farm with robots and hand it on. My worry is whether the farm still feeds a family or just a machine.
S4.do: Starts the co-op in year two or three once robots are tested elsewhere. Adds a side business with farm visits and robot demonstrations for schools and plans a handover to her son or a sale by sixty-five.
S4.feel: Calm and a bit excited, with some sadness that her hands won't be on the land at the end.
S4.quote: Somebody has to remember what a cow sounds like when she's calling her calf.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Jade becomes patient on purpose, letting others test the first machines, which she learned from broken cow collars. The school visits idea shows she wants to keep the old skills alive next to the new ones. She's calm but carries a quiet sadness about her own place in it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd lose Luis and I couldn't do anything clever about it. What would help is public money for farmer-owned robot co-ops, and proper retraining with pay for farmworkers, so it's not every farm for itself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people like me what we'd do with the time the robots save. I'd spend it on hedges and ponds and the stuff nobody pays for. A robot weeder could give me back the hours to look after the land properly.

headlineQuote: A robot weeder could give me back the hours to look after the land properly.
portrait: Jade Novak is a 58-year-old who farms sixty suckler cows and potatoes on ninety hectares she owns with her partner Owen, a carpenter. She checks an AI herd assistant before she pulls her boots on and is the person neighbours ring when their cow collars won't pair. She'd move early and together with other farms, buying robots through co-ops, and her steady worry is for her long-time farmworker, Luis. The two-year AGI picture makes her anxious because prices crash and she can't protect him, while five or ten years let her choose her road, train him as a technician and plan a handover.
biggestWorry: AGI within two years, because she would lose her farmworker Luis and couldn't do anything clever to prevent it.
whatWouldHelp: Public money for farmer-owned robot co-ops, and proper paid retraining for farmworkers so it isn't every farm for itself.
